newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries rally with focus on inflation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries rally with focus on inflation.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries, shrugging off evidence of robust growth in the fourth-quarter Gross Domestic Product, rallied on Friday on the lenient inflation signs the report contained, analysts said.
Players said the market was enclined to buy into the notion think structural changes in the U.S. economy now allowed healthy growth and full employment to coexist with unusually low price pressures.
The 30-year bond ended up one point and 1/32 at 96 11/32 to yield 6.79 percent, down from 6.87 percent late Thursday.
The rally kicked off soon after release of the October-December GDP, up a healthy 4.7 percent, while final sales rose an even stronger 4.9 percent.

But market players zeroed in on the two inflation gauges contained in the report -- the price index, up 1.8 percent, and the implicit price deflator, up 1.4 percent -- that both underscored the absence of worrisome inflationary pressures.

"The deflator and the price index looked very good," one bond trader at a European brokerage firm said. "People were short durations and did not want to remain so before an unemployment report they feel may be positive for the market."

The January employment report is set for release on February 7. The Reuters consensus forecast calls for the creation of 237,000 payrolls, a 5.2-percent jobless rate, and a 0.2-percent gain in average hourly earnings -- meaning the confirmation of the trend seen in recent months.
"Barring a surprise, the employment report should be supportive of the market," the bond trader added.

Buying was said to be led by the short-end and involve both retail and hedge funds. Another key feature was the extension in duration which gave both the 10-year note and the 30-year bond a healthy lift, traders said.
The market is not expecting a surprise from the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting on February 5-6 with virtually all U.S. forecasters predicting no change in monetary policy.

"The market may be sorry next week, but this week they are happy. GDP showed very little inflation," said senior economist Astrid Adolfson at MCM MoneyWatch, of the market's bet against a surprise on the rate or employment fronts.
"There is no justification for the Fed to move. (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan indicated as much," Adolfson added.
But Goldman, Sachs senior economist Ed McKelvey was cautious about the labor picture's implications for rates.
"Labor market tightness is national in scope," McKelvey noted. "All major occupational groups have seen some wage acceleration, though to varying degrees."

Though wage-led inflation is a risk usually associated with a low jobless rate and an aging business cycle, traders said the market was prepared to ignore the chances of a preemptive strike by the Fed.

They added the entire U.S. yield curve would suffer next week from a surprise hike in the federal funds rate which has been at 5.25 percent for exactly a year. Fed funds futures and the Eurodollars have not priced in a hike.

"The long end would suffer as well because of the carry trade," predicted one market strategist who noted the rising cost of borrowing funds to buy Treasuries hurt the credit market at almost all tightening moves in the 1990s.
The dollar, which held on to most of its recent gains, was cited as a positive factor for Treasuries.

Also posting gains on Friday were the two-year note, up 5/32 at 99-29/32 and 5.93 percent, the five-year, up 12/32 at 100/32 and 6.25 percent, and the 10-year note, up 20/32 at 100/32 and 6.50 percent.
